passage: At the international school in Singapore, the chemistry teacher posted a ranking after every test, names in order from first to twenty-eighth. Noa watched it change her class. Mei, who used to photocopy her notes for anyone, now kept her folder zipped inside her bag. Two friends who had shared lunch since Year 7 stopped sitting together after one of them overtook the other by a single mark. Then, in March, a different teacher set a group lab project with one shared grade. Noa noticed Mei unzip the folder again. Dev, who had been near the bottom of the list, explained the titration so clearly that the whole group clapped. Noa wondered which version of her classmates was the real one.

qa.q: What did the chemistry teacher post after every test?
qa.a: A ranking, names in order from first to twenty-eighth.

qa.q: What does Noa's wondering at the end suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: Noa seems puzzled and uneasy, troubled by how much the ranking changed her classmates' behaviour.

qa.q: What could the chemistry teacher change, based on what Noa saw?
qa.a: Drop the public ranking and use more shared-grade group work, so classmates have a reason to help each other.

qa.q: How might the ranking feel for Mei?
qa.a: Mei likely felt pressured and guarded, hiding notes she once shared freely, and was relieved to share again once the grade was shared.

grounding: A student notices a class ranking turning friends into rivals, while group work with a shared grade brings back mutual help.

passage: In the evening study hall of the coaching centre in Kota, the weekly rank list was pinned beside the water cooler. Bhavna noticed how people walked past it: quickly, eyes down, then back for a second look. Francis, ranked fourth, used to explain physics doubts to anyone who asked. This week, when Imtiaz asked him about lenses, Francis said, 'Figure it out, yaar,' and put on his headphones. Imtiaz was ranked fifth. At the next table, though, the students from the Sunday study circle, who didn't care much about ranks, were drawing ray diagrams together on one sheet, arguing and laughing. Bhavna looked at her own notes, tucked under her arm, and slowly slid them onto the table between her and her roommate.

qa.q: Where was the weekly rank list pinned?
qa.a: Beside the water cooler in the study hall.

qa.q: What does Bhavna sliding her notes onto the table suggest?
qa.a: Bhavna seems moved by the study circle's warmth and a little uncomfortable with her own guardedness, so she chooses to share.

qa.q: What could the centre try to reduce the rivalry Bhavna saw?
qa.a: Stop pinning ranks publicly and set up more study circles where students solve problems together.

qa.q: Why might Francis have refused Imtiaz this week?
qa.a: Francis may have felt threatened, since Imtiaz was ranked just below at fifth, and helping felt like giving away an edge.

grounding: A student sees a public rank list make classmates hide help, while a cooperative study circle shares freely.

passage: In Ms Aiko Mori's Grade 10 English class in Toronto, Rania read her poem aloud and pronounced the s in 'island'. Someone laughed, then half the room joined in, and Rania sat down with her face hot. Ms Mori didn't shout. At lunch she found Rania in the library. 'That laughter was wrong, and I should have stopped it sooner. How are you doing?' Rania shrugged, eyes wet. 'I just want to disappear.' 'Your poem was one of the strongest. Would you like to read it again sometime, or shall I?' The next morning Ms Mori began class without naming anyone. 'Yesterday we laughed at a mistake. In this room, we don't. English spelling is strange; ask me about "colonel" sometime.' A few students laughed, with her this time. Then Liam turned around. 'Your poem was good, Rania.'

qa.q: Which word did Rania mispronounce?
qa.a: 'Island'; she pronounced the s.

qa.q: What did Rania mean by 'I just want to disappear'?
qa.a: She felt humiliated and ashamed after the class laughed, and wanted to hide from everyone.

qa.q: Which of Ms Mori's steps helped repair things, and why?
qa.a: Speaking privately first and owning that she should have stopped it sooner, then naming the class norm the next day without naming anyone.

qa.q: How might Liam feel when turning around to Rania?
qa.a: Liam likely felt a bit guilty about the laughter and wanted to make amends, encouraged by the teacher's reset.

grounding: After a student is laughed at, a teacher speaks with her privately and resets the class norm without shaming anyone.

passage: At the district hockey academy, Damini missed an open goal in the practice match, and the coach shouted across the field, 'Did you leave your brain at home?' Some girls laughed. Yamini didn't. Damini finished practice without a word and skipped the team snack. The next morning, the coach called Damini aside by the equipment shed. 'What I said yesterday was out of line. You were brave to go for that shot. I'm sorry.' Damini nodded, not quite looking up. At the team huddle, the coach said, 'Yesterday I spoke badly to a player. Nobody here gets mocked for a miss, including by me. Misses are how shooters learn.' Yamini squeezed Damini's shoulder. That afternoon, Damini took the penalty stroke in the drill and scored.

qa.q: What did the coach shout when Damini missed?
qa.a: 'Did you leave your brain at home?'

qa.q: What does Damini skipping the team snack suggest?
qa.a: She felt humiliated and hurt after the shout and the laughter, and wanted to stay away from the team.

qa.q: What made the coach's repair work?
qa.a: The coach apologised to Damini privately, then set the team rule, including for the coach, without naming Damini.

qa.q: What is it like for Yamini, who didn't laugh?
qa.a: Yamini likely felt uncomfortable during the laughter and relieved at the apology, and shows support by squeezing Damini's shoulder.

grounding: A coach repairs a humiliating moment by apologising privately and resetting the team norm without shaming anyone.

passage:
Dear Rehana,
I'm writing because I didn't handle Friday well. When your phone rang during the test and I said, in front of everyone, 'Some people clearly don't care about their future,' I shamed you. I'm sorry. I found out afterwards that it was your mother calling from the hospital.

Yogesh Kulkarni
Physics

grounding: A teacher repairs a moment of public shaming with a private apology and a class-wide norm that names no one.

subtype: Speaking up in a large lecture [Actor]
passage: The economics lecture hall held two hundred students, and Professor Samir Rao spoke fast. Aadhya had been confused since the second slide: why did the demand curve shift, instead of just moving along? She wrote the question in the margin of her notebook, then crossed it out. Everyone else seemed to be nodding. Her neighbour was scrolling on his phone. The professor asked, 'Any questions?' The hall went silent. Aadhya's heart was pounding. She raised her hand. 'Sorry, this may be basic, but why does the curve shift here instead of moving along it?' The professor smiled. 'Not basic at all. Most people mix these up.' He redrew the graph. Afterwards, three students she had never spoken to stopped her at the door. 'Thank you. I was lost on that too.'

qa.q: How many students did the lecture hall hold?
qa.a: Two hundred.

qa.q: Why did Aadhya cross the question out at first?
qa.a: She felt anxious about seeming ignorant, since everyone else seemed to be nodding.

qa.q: What could Aadhya tell herself before the next lecture?
qa.a: That if something confuses her, others are probably confused too, so asking helps the whole hall.

qa.q: How do the three students at the door experience Aadhya's question?
qa.a: They were lost too, and felt relieved and grateful that someone asked.

grounding: A college student overcomes the fear of seeming ignorant in a big hall and finds others shared the question.

passage:

Amandeep

qa.a: They were probably grateful, since it cleared up something they also needed.

subtype: Training or class culture as a young teacher [Actor]
passage: Jeevan's first training batch at the customer-service centre began with a dead projector and twenty-two trainees who had been kept waiting forty minutes. Jeevan, younger than half of them, wrote on the whiteboard instead. Ten minutes in, Savita answered a practice question wrong, and Shankar, a loud older trainee, called out, 'Madam, go back to school!' A few people laughed. Jeevan's heart raced; it would be easy to laugh along and be liked. Instead: 'Shankar, no comments on answers here. Savita, good try. What made you choose that?' Later, when Shankar asked a sharp, useful question, Jeevan thanked him in the same even voice. By the end of the day, people were calling out answers freely, even the wrong ones.

qa.a: Because the projector was dead.

qa.q: How did Jeevan set a fair tone with Shankar?
qa.a: By stopping the comment calmly and firmly, then thanking Shankar for a useful question later in the same even voice, so one rule applied to everyone.

qa.q: How might Savita feel after Jeevan's response?
qa.a: She likely felt protected and less embarrassed, with her attempt valued instead of mocked.

grounding: A young trainer, under a rough start, sets the room's tone through calm, fair responses to the first mistake and first interruption.

subtype: Training or class culture as a young teacher [Actor]
passage: On his first day at a Bengaluru school, Gautam wrote the area of a circle as 2πr on the board. A girl in the front row put up her hand. 'Sir, isn't that the circumference?' The class went still, waiting to see what he'd do. Gautam looked, laughed at himself and said, 'Good catch. It's π r squared. Keep checking me.' Twenty minutes later, Tanvir, known as the class topper, started talking over a classmate's answer. Gautam said evenly, 'Tanvir, let Deepti finish, then you're next.' The class exchanged glances; the old teachers had let Tanvir say anything. At the end of the week, Gautam sent the same note home for two talkers: Tanvir and a boy from the back row. Some students grumbled that the new sir was strict. But hands went up more often.

qa.q: What did Gautam wrongly write on the board?
qa.a: 2πr as the area of a circle.

qa.q: Why did the class go still after the girl's question?
qa.a: They were curious and a little nervous, waiting to see if the new teacher would be embarrassed or angry at being corrected.

qa.q: Which of Gautam's choices set a fair tone?
qa.a: Owning the mistake openly, and applying the same rule to the topper as to a boy from the back row.

qa.q: How might Tanvir experience the new teacher?
qa.a: Tanvir, used to being allowed to say anything, may feel surprised and a bit put out at being told to wait.

grounding: A young teacher sets the class tone by owning the first mistake and handling the first interruption fairly, even if it costs popularity.

qa.a: Over three weekends.

qa.a: He felt angry and helpless, staring at the table with a hot face while Maria took the praise.

qa.a: Dilip sees the credit-taking and stays quiet at first, then helps with advice and is pleased when Joseph gets the credit.

grounding: Over a week a junior moves from anger at a senior taking credit to calmly raising it with documented evidence.

passage: First week of April: Bidisha, new to the marketing team, started having lunch with people from sales and finance. She asked about their targets and remembered their children's names. It was friendly and useful. Mid-April: the promotion list was coming. When Nazia's campaign numbers came in low, Bidisha mentioned it to the director over coffee, 'just so you're not surprised', but left out that the budget had been cut halfway. She felt a small rush, and then a small knot in her stomach. End of May: the director praised Bidisha in the team meeting. Nazia sat three seats away, not looking up. Later, a finance colleague mentioned the budget cut in passing, and the director turned to look at Bidisha for a long moment.

qa.q: What did Bidisha leave out when mentioning Nazia's numbers?
qa.a: That the budget had been cut halfway.

qa.q: What did Bidisha feel after the coffee with the director?
qa.a: A small rush of excitement, followed by a knot of guilt in her stomach.

qa.q: Where did Bidisha cross from normal networking into harm, and what could she have done instead?
qa.a: When she hid the budget cut to make Nazia look bad; she could have kept building contacts honestly and let her own work speak.

qa.q: What is it like for Nazia in the May meeting?
qa.a: Nazia sits not looking up while Bidisha is praised, likely feeling hurt and undermined.

grounding: Over two months an ambitious employee moves from normal networking to shaping impressions by hiding facts, with consequences.

passage: Rashmi, you're asking how to get noticed? Sit, and let old Rukmini tell you something. In 1998 I was a sharp young officer at the textile corporation, hungry to rise. I made friends in every department. I remembered birthdays, I carried sweets to the accounts section. That was fine; people liked me, and I liked them. But when the deputy manager post opened, I went further. My colleague Suresh had made a costing error, and he fixed it in time. I made sure the general manager heard about the error and not the fix. I got the post. Suresh stopped greeting me. Later the general manager learned the full story and never trusted me with anything important again. Build friendships, child. Just don't build them on someone else's back.

qa.q: What did Suresh do after making the costing error?
qa.a: He fixed it in time.

qa.q: What might Suresh have felt when he stopped greeting Rukmini?
qa.a: Suresh likely felt betrayed and angry that Rukmini had told only half the story to win the post.

qa.q: Which choice in the story turned Rukmini's networking harmful?
qa.a: Making sure the general manager heard about Suresh's error but not the fix; the friendships were fine, but hiding facts to undermine Suresh was not.

qa.q: How did the general manager see Rukmini after learning the full story?
qa.a: The general manager stopped trusting Rukmini with anything important, seeing the promotion as unfairly won.

grounding: A senior recalls how friendly networking was fine until hiding a colleague's fix to rise cost lasting trust.

passage: The audit was at nine the next morning, the office air-conditioning had failed, and half the team had gone home sweaty and grumpy. Wasim stayed, partly to finish and partly because he knew the regional manager, Mr Bakshi, noticed who stayed. He brought Mr Bakshi tea and chatted about cricket; that part felt fine. Then, checking the shared folder, he spotted a wrong total in Tanvir's section. Tanvir was his main rival for team lead. It would be easy to say nothing and let the auditors find it, or to mention it to Mr Bakshi now, casually, as Tanvir's carelessness. Wasim sat with it in the heat. Then he picked up his phone and messaged Tanvir: 'Row 48 total looks off. Fixing it with a note so you can check.' Tanvir replied with a thumbs-up at 11:40.

qa.q: What did Wasim spot in Tanvir's section?
qa.a: A wrong total, in row 48.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling as he sat with the error?
qa.a: Wasim felt tempted and torn, seeing an easy way to beat a rival, and uneasy about what that would mean.

qa.q: Which of Wasim's choices were fair networking, and which would have crossed a line?
qa.a: Staying late and chatting with Mr Bakshi is normal; hiding the error or using it to make Tanvir look careless would have undermined a colleague.

qa.q: How might Tanvir feel getting the late-night message?
qa.a: Tanvir likely felt relieved and grateful, and may trust Wasim more despite the rivalry.

grounding: Under deadline pressure, an ambitious employee builds goodwill with a manager but stops short of undermining a rival.

passage: At the cooperative dairy office in a small town near Anand, two camps had formed: those loyal to the old secretary and those backing the new chairman. Farhan, the young accounts clerk, kept his head down and ate lunch alone at his desk. It didn't work. On Monday, the secretary's men asked him to delay the chairman's expense files. On Tuesday, the chairman's nephew asked him to 'find something' in the secretary's accounts. Farhan said no to both, politely. By Thursday, neither side greeted him, and his leave application had been 'lost'. That evening Sumit, the older milk-testing officer, sat beside him at the bus stand. 'You did right. But you need people who know it. Talk to the auditor, and keep copies of every request.' Farhan nodded, feeling less alone.

qa.q: What did the chairman's nephew ask Farhan to do?
qa.a: To 'find something' in the secretary's accounts.

qa.q: How did Farhan feel by Thursday?
qa.a: He felt isolated and unprotected, with neither side greeting him and his leave application 'lost'.

qa.q: What did Sumit suggest, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Talking to the auditor and keeping copies of every request, so Farhan's neutrality has quiet allies and a record to protect him.

qa.q: How might the secretary's men see Farhan's polite refusal?
qa.a: They likely see it as disloyalty rather than principle, which is why they stop greeting him.

grounding: A clerk who stays out of two rival camps is pressed by both and left unprotected until a quiet ally advises him.

passage: At the architecture firm in Melbourne, the two senior partners had stopped speaking, and every junior was expected to pick a side. Mei didn't. She worked on projects for both, answered both politely and skipped the Friday drinks where each camp gathered. For a while she felt proud of it. Then the hospital project ran late, each partner blamed the other's team, and both named Mei as the one who had dropped the ball. Neither defended her. That night she sat in the car park, gripping the steering wheel. Jamal, from the planning team, knocked on the window. 'I saw the emails. You weren't the delay. Want me to go through the timeline with you and the office manager tomorrow?' Mei let out a long breath. 'Yes. Please.'

qa.q: Which project ran late?
qa.a: The hospital project.

qa.q: What does Mei gripping the steering wheel suggest?
qa.a: She felt hurt, alone and trapped, blamed by both partners with no one defending her.

qa.q: What does Mei need now, and how is Jamal offering it?
qa.a: A clear, quiet ally; Jamal offers to go through the timeline with her and the office manager to show she wasn't the delay.

qa.q: What might Jamal see that the partners ignore?
qa.a: Jamal has read the emails and sees that Mei wasn't the delay, and that her neutrality left her without protection.

grounding: An employee staying out of a partners' feud is blamed by both sides and needs a quiet ally with the facts.

passage: On Ward 6 of the district hospital, the two senior sisters had been feuding since the new duty roster. Sister Grace's nurses took the morning tea break together; Sister Philomena's took theirs after. Urmila, a staff nurse in her second year, drank her tea standing at the medicine trolley, belonging to neither group. On Wednesday, Grace asked her to report that Philomena's shift had left the drug register unsigned. On Thursday, Philomena asked her to say Grace had swapped shifts without permission. Urmila said she would only report what she had seen herself. Both sisters went cold, and her night shifts somehow doubled. Uma, the ward clerk, noticed the roster and quietly showed Urmila how to request a formal review through the nursing superintendent. 'Put it in writing,' Uma said. 'Neutral is safer on paper.'

qa.q: Where did Urmila drink her tea?
qa.a: Standing at the medicine trolley.

qa.q: What might Urmila be feeling after both sisters went cold?
qa.a: Likely anxious and exposed, since her principled neutrality brought doubled night shifts and no protection.

qa.q: How does Uma's advice help Urmila?
qa.a: Requesting a formal roster review in writing through the nursing superintendent gives Urmila protection and a record, instead of relying on either camp.

qa.q: How might Sister Grace see Urmila's refusal?
qa.a: Grace likely sees it as siding with Philomena, since in a feud neutrality can look like disloyalty.

grounding: A nurse who refuses to join either side of a ward feud is squeezed by both and needs a quiet ally and a written record.

passage:
Journal, Tuesday, 11:40 p.m.
Week two at the agency. Things I've noticed that nobody else seems to:
1. Nobody leaves before the boss, and the boss leaves at ten.
2. When the client presentation had a typo today, the boss asked, 'Whose slide?' before asking how to fix it. Three people looked at the floor.
3. Jaya, who's been here two years, eats lunch at her desk with one hand and types with the other. When I asked if she ever takes a full lunch, she laughed. 'Lunch is for people with small targets.'
4. Everyone says 'it's crazy but it's fun'. Nobody looks like they're having fun.
I'm writing this down because I can feel myself getting used to it. Yesterday I apologised for leaving at nine.
Reena

qa.q: At what time does the boss leave?
qa.a: At ten.

qa.q: Why is Reena writing these things down?
qa.a: Reena feels uneasy and a little alarmed, sensing the slide into accepting it after apologising for leaving at nine.

qa.q: What could help Reena keep seeing clearly?
qa.a: Keep the journal, protect a few fixed limits like a proper lunch, and talk with a trusted friend or mentor outside the agency.

qa.q: How might Jaya see her own habits?
qa.a: Jaya seems to see skipping lunch as normal, even a badge of big targets, after two years of blending in.

grounding: A newcomer sees long hours, fear and blame clearly while colleagues treat them as ordinary, and notices herself adapting.

passage: In the office of the sugar mill outside Kolhapur, Chetan, three weeks into his first job, noticed things the others no longer seemed to. The clerks arrived at eight and left only after the manager's jeep drove away, sometimes at nine at night. When a weighbridge slip went missing, the manager shouted in the corridor, and within minutes three people had blamed the tanker driver, who wasn't even there. Dhruv, who had joined only a year before Chetan, said, 'Don't take it to heart, that's just how he is.' He said it the way people talk about rain. At the tea stall, Chetan watched Dhruv flinch every time the jeep horn sounded. On the bus home, Chetan typed in his phone notes: 'Week three. Still shocked. Don't stop being shocked.'

qa.q: Who did three people blame for the missing weighbridge slip?
qa.a: The tanker driver, who wasn't even there.

qa.q: What does Chetan's phone note suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: Chetan feels shocked and uneasy, and worried about getting used to it like everyone else.

qa.q: What could Chetan do to keep his clear view without putting himself at risk?
qa.a: Keep noting what he sees, find one or two colleagues who also feel uneasy, and talk to a trusted mentor outside the mill.

qa.q: How might Dhruv be experiencing the culture after a year?
qa.a: Dhruv talks about it like the weather but flinches at the jeep horn, so he is likely still afraid underneath, just used to hiding it.

grounding: A newcomer sees long hours, fear and blame clearly while a colleague who has blended in treats them as normal.
